#4726. Here are the coolest e-motorcycles and gear we saw at EICMA 2026

Every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase. That means that all of the newest electric motorcycle announcements happen in one place, and we get a chance to check out the coolest developments and most interesting new gear.

Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.

LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the company has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.

The new S4 Honcho family was a major focus, including the street-oriented Honcho Street, off-road Honcho Trail, and newly unveiled Honcho Skate, a stripped-down addition to the modular platform. The booth also included LiveWire’s larger S2 electric motorcycles, creating a pretty broad spectrum from lightweight urban machines up through full-size highway-capable electric motorcycles.

The other big piece of the booth was DUST Moto, which LiveWire acquired earlier this year. The production-intent DUST Hightail was displayed alongside the newly revealed DUST Spur, giving LiveWire an immediate presence in the increasingly popular lightweight electric dirt bike category.

Add in STACYC’s electric balance bikes for young riders, and the entire booth almost looked like an electric two-wheeler progression chart: start a kid on a STACYC, move up through lightweight DUST and Honcho machines, and eventually graduate to a full-size LiveWire.

GR1T Motorcycles is a relatively young European electric motorcycle startup that caught my eye at EICMA with its G1 platform, a lightweight electric motorcycle designed and engineered in Italy. The basic recipe is pretty compelling: 130 km/h (81 mph) top speed, 11 kW of continuous power and 26.6 kW (36 hp) peak, all while weighing just 130 kg (287 lb).

Perhaps most importantly for urban riders, its roughly 6 kWh battery is actually split into two removable 3 kWh packs, meaning apartment dwellers can pull the batteries out and charge them inside. They’re big, but removing them is doable.

GR1T’s bikes therefore pack in around 50% more battery capacity than most electric motorcycles in this size and weight class, meaning roughly 50% more range, as well.

There are also some interesting and clever design choices, like the underslung rear suspension and the triple-camera system that includes front and rear dashcams plus a cockpit-facing camera for recording the rider.

The clever part of the overall design scheme is that GR1T isn’t developing a separate platform for every motorcycle. The same basic G1 chassis, motor, batteries, belt drive, and electronics underpin four versions: the G1S Street, G1X Scrambler, G1XR Raider, and utility-oriented G1M Mission.

Prices are set to start at €8,495 including VAT, putting these squarely in that emerging category of reasonably affordable, lightweight electric motorcycles that have enough speed for real-world commuting without chasing superbike performance.

There’s an important caveat, though: these aren’t production motorcycles yet. GR1T says it is currently fundraising, with factory development and pre-orders set to follow after funding closes and first deliveries now targeted for the first half of 2028.

So the bikes aren’t quite ready for primetime yet, but it’s definitely a company to watch.

Real Motors brought one of the more visually striking electric motorcycles to EICMA with Project: ARES, a futuristic electric café racer that the American startup describes as an “Electric Analog” machine – basically an attempt to preserve the raw, mechanical connection of motorcycling while ditching unnecessary screens and gadgetry.

And there’s plenty of performance underneath the sci-fi bodywork: Real Motors lists a 75 kW (100 hp) motor, a 15 kWh battery, a 120 mph (192 km/h) top speed, and an estimated weight of 485 lb (220 kg).

The analog analogy is spot on, with the display probably the simplest and most straightforward I’ve ever seen on an electric motorcycle. There’s also no app, no subscription, and no digital handcuffs. The bike is very much the electric equivalent of a simple ICE bike that just rides, albeit with a much nicer ride.

Unlike many of the futuristic concepts scattered around EICMA, ARES is actually headed toward limited production.

Real Motors plans to build just 250 examples in its first LOT 01 production run, with pricing starting at $20,000 and North American deliveries targeted for early 2027. European deliveries are expected after homologation is completed.

The company has also brought former LiveWire CTO Vance Strader onto the project as it makes the difficult transition from a very cool prototype into an actual production motorcycle.

I actually had the chance to do a spin on the bike, and so I’ll be reporting back on the experience. But you can tell from my smile below that the ride was quite an experience!

Seatylock has been my go-to e-bike lock company for several years now, and I use their locks for my several e-bikes and my wife’s e-bike too.

Now Seatylock has returned with some even more impressive locks. The company showed off its new Ultra D28 lock, which is both angle grinder-proof and wide enough to lock the wheel of a motorcycle. It solves the problem of how do you make a lock strong enough for a motorcycle but also small and light enough that you can actually carry it with you, unlike a massive chain lock that usually stays where you park your motorcycle overnight.

In the image below, you can see the shackle next to an exposed section demonstrating the diamond coating that essentially destroys angle grinder discs – even diamond coated discs.

The company also has a slightly smaller version of the same lock designed for bicycles.

Both will absolutely destroy even the toughest angle grinder discs. Sure, eventually someone could cut through them, but it may take a dozen discs and by that point the thief has moved on to an easier target.

At EICMA 2026, Royal Enfield continued expanding its electric motorcycle ambitions with its Flying Flea sub-brand, showcasing the scrambler-style motorcycle alongside its growing lineup of lightweight, retro-inspired electric motorcycles.

There were several interesting colorways and customized designs on display, showcasing the Flying Flea’s stylish design.

The new models blend Royal Enfield’s classic design heritage with modern electric technology, targeting urban riders and those looking for a fun, approachable electric motorcycle rather than a high-performance machine.

With distinctive styling, compact proportions, and an emphasis on accessible riding, the Flying Flea lineup represents Royal Enfield’s effort to carve out a place in the emerging market for smaller electric motorcycles while maintaining the character that has made its gasoline-powered bikes so popular.

Yamaha showed off its new NMAX E electric scooter, bringing battery-powered performance to one of the brand’s most recognizable urban scooter families.

Designed as an electric alternative to the popular gasoline-powered NMAX, the new model combines familiar sporty styling with a quiet, low-maintenance electric drivetrain aimed at everyday city commuting.

The NMAX E uses Yamaha’s new compact eAxle powertrain, shared with the larger-wheeled XENTER E, and delivers up to 7.5 kW (10 hp) of peak power, putting it in the 125cc-equivalent class.

With its practical step-through design, automatic operation, and approachable performance, the NMAX E represents another step in Yamaha’s push to electrify its urban mobility lineup, particularly in European markets where scooters are already a popular alternative to cars.

Segway showed off a new vision for safer electric scooters, including its futuristic X Cruiser concept that takes rider protection to a whole new level.

Rather than relying solely on traditional motorcycle safety equipment, the X Cruiser explores automotive-inspired features such as integrated seats with seatbelts, partial enclosures, and even a fully roofed version designed to offer additional protection from the elements.

The concept includes several configurations, ranging from a more conventional open scooter to a partially enclosed design and a fully covered model that looks like a cross between a motorcycle and a tiny electric car. While these designs are still concepts rather than production-ready scooters, they demonstrate how Segway is rethinking two-wheeled transportation by exploring ways to make electric scooters safer, more comfortable, and potentially more appealing to riders who might otherwise be hesitant to trade four wheels for two.

Eli Electric Vehicles took to EICMA 2026 to display its compact Eli Zero electric quadricycle, a tiny two-seat urban EV designed to offer much of the convenience of a car without the size, weight, or expense of a conventional automobile.

With its enclosed cabin, side-by-side seating, and ultra-compact footprint, the Eli Zero offers a practical alternative to larger vehicles for short city trips, combining the weather protection and comfort of a car with the maneuverability and efficiency of a much smaller vehicle.

The company revealed a more powerful L7e-class version of the Eli Zero that it had previously teased, expanding the vehicle’s capabilities beyond its existing L6e configuration. The new Race Edition also pushes the envelope farther with custom interior and a few extra accents to the body.

With growing interest in smaller, more efficient urban transportation, Eli’s presence at EICMA definitely underlined how the show is increasingly embracing electric mobility solutions that go beyond traditional motorcycles and scooters.

NIU showed off its latest lineup of electric scooters, continuing the brand’s push to make battery-powered two-wheelers a practical alternative to gasoline-powered urban transportation. Known for its sleek designs, connected technology, and approachable electric scooters, NIU highlighted models aimed at a range of riders, from everyday city commuters to those looking for more powerful machines capable of keeping up with faster urban traffic.

The company showed off several new models for the 2027 model year, with scooters that combine modern styling with features such as smartphone connectivity, smart security systems, and efficient electric drivetrains, all while maintaining the simplicity and low operating costs that make electric scooters so appealing.

While I didn’t see anything groundbreaking at the brand’s booth this year, the incremental updates look to push new tech features further throughout the brand’s many models, helping more of NIU’s offerings enter that premium level that the company has been known for.

For something a bit wilder, Honda shared its futuristic EV Outlier Concept, an electric motorcycle that explores what two-wheeled design could look like when engineers are freed from the constraints of traditional gasoline-powered motorcycles.

With its long, low-slung profile, radically different riding position, and futuristic bodywork, the EV Outlier looks more like something out of a science fiction movie than a conventional motorcycle. The concept features electric motors integrated into both wheels, giving it two-wheel drive while opening up new possibilities for packaging and weight distribution.

Rather than simply replacing a combustion engine with a battery and motor, Honda used the EV Outlier to rethink the entire motorcycle layout, demonstrating how electrification could lead to entirely new types of riding experiences.

While the bike remains a design concept with no announced production plans, it offers an intriguing glimpse into Honda’s vision for the future of electric motorcycles.

Vespa showed off its next-generation electric scooter lineup at EICMA, including electric versions of the Primavera, Sprint S, and Primavera Tech. While they don’t look radically different, there’s a lot more happening underneath the familiar steel bodywork.

A new Italian-made, rare-earth-free electric motor improves efficiency and performance, while the 45 km/h Primavera and Sprint S now feature removable batteries.

The faster 67 km/h Primavera Tech gets up to 90 km of WMTC range – a 12.5% improvement – along with an updated vehicle management system and more efficient charger.

#4725. Divers release first footage of SS ‘United States’ after intentional sinking

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 2:00 PM EST

It took a few hours longer than expected, but the SS United States now rests at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico. The nearly 1,000-foot-long ocean liner sank off the coast of Pensacola, Florida, to a depth of about 190 feet on November 11, where it is now officially the world’s largest artificial reef. In the years ahead, biologists and conservationists will monitor the vessel’s remains as numerous marine species slowly convert the ship into their own home.

Ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition. On November 13, the team released a brief video of their successful excursion. Interestingly, the footage shows the ship is resting upright on the ocean floor despite initially sinking on its side.

“It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet. “It was very cleaned up. I mean, you could see people really took their time to clean it really nicely.”

The project marks the first time ecologists will be able to monitor a shipwreck’s transformation in real-time. Researchers now plan to conduct annual visits to the SS United States to chart not only the artificial reef’s progress, but how the ship’s materials may affect the surrounding ocean conditions.

In its heyday, the SS United States was the world’s fastest ocean liner. Larger than the RMS Titanic, she was the most powerful, advanced, and modern passenger liner when she first took to the ocean in 1952. In addition to the 1,700 passengers, 7,935 quarts of ice cream and 500 pounds of caviar were also on board. During that maiden voyage (July 3-7, 1952), she broke the transatlantic speed record held by the RMS Queen Mary by over 10 hours. The United States made the crossing from the United Kingdom to New York in three days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes at an average speed of 40.96 mph.

She was designed by naval architect William Francis Gibbs (August 24, 1886 – September 6, 1967), and was built to be converted into a troopship if the United States Navy needed during a time of war. But she never was called into military service. Instead, the United States transported immigrants and celebrities, including future President and First Lady John and Jacqueline Kennedy, actors Grace Kelly, Gary Cooper, and Marilyn Monroe, artist Salvador Dali, and musicians Duke Ellington and Irving Berlin. Walt Disney even filmed parts of the 1962 comedy Bon Voyage aboard the ship.

An engineering marvel, some of the key design features were in the rudder, radar mast, and propellers.

The rudder was designed for good maneuverability at high speeds. The Titanic’s relatively small rudder was one factor behind the ship’s collision with an iceberg and tragic sinking in 1912.

The SS United States had the latest radar equipment, which allowed the crew to see the locations of  other ships and objects in the ocean despite the weather. It was among the first ocean liners to use radar, which was located at one of the highest points on the ship, so in addition to her radar “eyes,” a lookout could be stationed there to warn the captain of any danger in the ship’s path.

Considered a top-secret design, the ship had four propellers—two with four blades and two with five. According to the SS United States Conservancy, this configuration was tested and selected for its superior hydrodynamic performance. The propeller design was overseen by a pioneering Gibbs & Cox engineer named Elaine Kaplan.

Ocean liners became a less attractive option once air travel became quicker and less expensive. The SS United States ceased operations in 1969, and stayed in drydock in several cities before becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.

#4724. Meet “Sister," the Free, 24/7 Caregiver Who Is Your Sister

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Who ends up caring for aging parents? Suddenly, people are talking about it after a fake Saturday Night Live ad spotlighted the issue.

Last week, SNL rolled out a parody pitch for “Sister,” a “live-in, 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free and also your sister.” The brothers in the ad get their lives back. Sister? She quits her job, breaks her lease, and moves halfway across the country to care for her incapacitated father.

The joke hit a nerve. Within days, more than 7 million people had watched it on YouTube, and thousands of women commented that they were some version of “I am Sister.” One woman wrote, "Feels like you talked directly to my brothers." Another commented, "This was so real it almost gave me a stroke from rage." Then, last Friday, the New York Times picked up where the sketch left off with a front-page story, “An SNL Sketch Hits Close to Home for Many,” on the gender gap in caregiving.

“Sister” is one more place where women’s unpaid labor goes unnoticed. SNL may have found the topic funny, but the numbers are hard to laugh off:

61 percent of family caregivers of adults are women, compared to 38 percent who are men.

Nearly 25 percent of women caregivers provide around-the-clock care, compared with 15 percent of men (AARP).

Family caregivers lose an average of $120,500 over a lifetime in wages, retirement income, and Social Security benefits (AARP).

The value of that care? $1.01 trillion a year, more than the United States spent on Medicare benefits in 2025 (AARP).

Medicare generally doesn’t cover ongoing help with bathing, dressing, or getting to the bathroom. A home health aide costs roughly $6,688 a month in 2025. Most families can’t swing that, so the work falls to relatives and, as the sketch suggests, to daughters.

But the brothers in the ad never call it work. One cheerfully says Sister isn’t confused by the medications, or if she is, “she hasn’t brought it up to me, because I haven’t asked.” When labor happens quietly, at home and without a paycheck, the people who benefit can go years without noticing it.

In 2017, Stanford researchers writing in JAMA Neurology called out this inequity. They noted that 83 percent of caregiving comes from unpaid sources, meaning family, and that the average person with dementia needs 171 hours of care per month. Their verdict: “The best long-term care insurance in our country is a conscientious daughter.”

No wonder the SNL ad resonated. Sisters saddled with caregiving resent the lopsided split, and the data backs them up. In November of 2026, Bay Alarm Medical, a provider of medical alert systems and senior safety solutions, surveyed 1,008 U.S. adults who share or once shared care for a parent over 65 and found that 47 percent resent a sibling because caregiving wasn’t divided fairly.

A study from Purdue University and the University of Missouri found that sibling tension climbs when a parent has cognitive impairment, especially among the siblings doing the caring. Non-caregivers often seemed unaware of the situation and stayed out of it to dodge conflict. Earlier research tells the same story from both sides: The sibling doing the most feels frustration and anger toward those doing less, while the less-involved feel guilty.

This helps explain why the last stage of a parent’s life is one of the most perilous for siblings. One of the most significant findings in a June 2026 survey by Bay Alarm was that 18 percent reported that they had lost a relationship with a sibling because of disagreements over caring for an aging parent.

An Aging Life Care Manager can help families navigate disagreements and develop a plan that respects the parent's wishes. Lina Supnet-Zapata, the incoming president of the Aging Life Care Association, knows personally the caregiving challenges for siblings. "After my father passed away," she says, "my siblings and I disagreed so much about what our mother's care should look like that we didn't speak for almost six months. Those arguments nearly destroyed our relationships."

Now Supnet-Zapata helps families address these thorny problems. She describes a “default daughter trap,” where one capable daughter quietly becomes the family’s entire care plan. It has three moving parts:

Invisible labor. She answers the calls, tracks medications, spots behavioral changes, coordinates providers, and translates medical updates for everyone else.

The competence penalty. She’s great at logistics, so relatives assume her capacity is unlimited and step back.

Personal erosion. Carrying the load silently disturbs her career momentum, her physical and mental health, her marriage, and her ability to enjoy being a daughter instead of a case manager.

Supnet-Zapata offers three practical moves for caregivers:

Replace vague offers with concrete tasks. “Let me know if you need anything” isn’t enough. Ask siblings to name the specific responsibilities they will do.

Build a backup plan before a crisis. Organize legal, financial, and medical records early, and line up backup caregivers so everything doesn’t collapse when the primary daughter is unavailable.

Practice self-compassion. Drop the perfectionism and have realistic expectations. "The biggest thing I want families to understand is that being a good caregiver doesn't mean doing everything yourself," she says. "Getting help can be one of the best things you do for both your parent and yourself."

Still, given cultural norms, women will likely be the ones to need this guidance since they will continue to orchestrate care. And the SNL ad shows viewers exactly how care became “women’s work.” A “scientist” in the sketch explains: “Years of internalized sexism warped Sister’s brain into thinking that caregiving is her responsibility."

When a brother texts, "Dad fell," Sister is instantly activated. Then, the ad tells brothers, "You’re done for life. See you at the funeral.”

#4722. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.

#4721. Robo-frog swims with liquid crystal muscles powered by light

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 3:00 PM EST

A silicone frog built by engineers at Denmark’s Aarhus University can’t swim nearly as fast as its amphibian inspiration, but it still manages to get the job done without any moving parts. The odd invention owes its slow-but-steady aquatic maneuvering to a set of six artificial muscles specially designed to contract when exposed to near-infrared light.

The team’s novel system is detailed in a study recently published in the journal Advanced Materials Technologies. Although similar setups may one day boost the capabilities of soft robots tasked with search and rescue or environmental monitoring, its creators are a bit more realistic about this frog-bot’s near-term uses.

“I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, said in a profile. “I think people would have fun playing with a frog like this using a suitable light source.”

Each of the robot’s muscles is built using crystal elastomers. These materials are specifically manufactured to contract while they are heating, and then revert back to their original shape once cooled. In this case, Ryberg and her collaborators also added a molecule that converts near-infrared light into heat. This allows the muscles to tighten after directly exposing them to a lamp. That said, the process isn’t as simple as sticking the elastomers onto their model frog and dropping it into water.

“Getting the six muscles to work together was a major challenge,” explained Brigitte Städler, a study co-author and Aarhus University chemist. “If they don’t contract in a coordinated way, the frog won’t swim forwards. It may simply spin around.”

A lot of trial-and-error also went into concocting the elastomers themselves. In addition to contracting properly, the material needed the proper consistency to use in a 3D printer. To do this, Ryberg experimented with various molecular ingredients and molecule chain lengths to perfect the robot muscle recipe.

“In a conventional 3D printer, you typically melt a solid plastic filament. Our material is more like very thick syrup or icing that you squeeze through a piping bag when decorating a cake,” said Ryberg.

The final result is a light-powered soft robot that’s quite unique, but also not in any hurry. At its best pace, the frog swam a little over three inches in about two minutes. That may not get it to its destination quickly, but the proof-of-concept successfully offers a new way to think about robotic design, and the ways engineers can power their creations. Until then, there is always the potential for robo-frog toys.

#4720. Tesla stops selling every Cybertruck except the $109,990 Cyberbeast

Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.

The Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected. So the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today costs $109,990, up 57% from $69,990 in early August.

Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator shows today with a Los Angeles delivery address:

A week ago, the Cyberbeast cost $102,490. Before that, it was $99,990. That’s a $10,000 (10%) increase in about a week on a truck that hasn’t changed: 320 miles of estimated range, 11,000 lbs of towing, and 0-60 mph in 2.6 seconds.

On November 6, the same day Elon Musk announced the end of Cybertruck production, Tesla raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. That made the $92,490 Premium AWD the entry point. Now it’s gone too, with no announcement. The configurator just stopped letting you pick it.

New inventory isn’t an alternative either. When we checked, Tesla’s inventory search showed no new Cybertrucks within 200 miles of Los Angeles.

This comes two days after Musk extended Cybertruck production through the end of summer 2027 to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” On Monday, he claimed the order rate “far exceeds” production and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.”

If there really is a backlog, cutting off the two cheaper trims is one way to cap it before the line shuts down. It also pushes whatever demand is left toward the most expensive, highest-margin version of the truck.

But the sales data doesn’t describe a truck with a demand problem in the other direction. We estimate Tesla delivered 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks in Q3, a pace of about 30,000 a year on a line with more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. And in February, Tesla was offering a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 for “only the next 10 days.”

That’s $50,000 less than the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today. Nine months later.

Some of those $59,990 buyers are still waiting on delivery dates pushed into 2027. Tesla hasn’t said whether their orders, or any other Dual Motor and Premium orders in the queue, will be built before production ends.

Unlike the thousands of $59k CT orders that may never get manufactured I can guarantee that every high margin $110k CyberBeast order will be delivered before production ends.

This is the wind-down playbook, and it’s moving faster than I expected. Announce the end, raise prices, pull the cheaper trims, and sell the last trucks in their most expensive form. Tesla is squeezing as much as it can out of every remaining Cybertruck.

I don’t blame Tesla for wanting margin on a program it’s walking away from. But it makes the “order backlog” talk look like what we said it was: an end-of-life rush Tesla created by announcing the end, now being monetized with a $109,990 sticker. Not great for anyone who was told in 2019 that this truck would start at $39,900, or that the tri-motor version would cost $69,900.

If you want a Cybertruck that isn’t a Cyberbeast, you’re now shopping used. And I’d keep an eye on used prices, because a truck that’s going out of production with no cheaper new option could hold its value better than it has over the last two years.

#4719. Nihilism Is Not What You Think

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

Since Friedrich Nietzsche, philosophers have grappled with the question of how to respond to nihilism. Nihilism, often used as a derogatory term for a "life-denying," destructive, and perhaps most of all depressive philosophy, is what drove existentialists to write about the right response to a meaningless universe devoid of purpose. This is why I've published an academic article on the topic. As nihilism is commonly used as a derogatory term, even in the works of Friedrich Nietzsche, it will prove helpful for the purpose of this post to take a "value-neutral" view on nihilism and achieve conceptual clarity of the term nihilism, beyond some sort of "life-denying" philosophy.

I define nihilism narrowly as the negative and eliminativist thesis of denying objective values. Moral nihilism, therefore, refers to the meta-ethical thesis that there is no objective morality, no inherent goodness or wrongness, a view that many existentialists agree with. The concern here, however, is existential nihilism, which can be defined as the denial of life being meaningful and the universe having a purpose. Whether moral and existential nihilism entail each other is beyond the scope of this post, but they at least stand in a close relation.

Existentialists are by definition, therefore, all existential nihilists, though not necessarily moral nihilists or atheists. As is commonly joked about existentialist thinkers, with the exception of Sartre, they do not appreciate being labelled as existentialists. Just like moral nihilism is often negatively associated and equated with immoralism, existential nihilism is often associated with destructive behaviour and suicide. These positions, however, should not be confused or seen as standing in a necessary causal relationship.

Existential nihilism, despite its negative connotations, should therefore not be seen as a label, but rather as something that is taken as a fact or at least a widespread view in the modern world, from which existential philosophy takes off. The popularity and critical acclaim of contemporary works such as BoJack Horseman, True Detective, and Rick and Morty exploring existential nihilism make it one of the most popular philosophical views in folk philosophy.

In his defence of scientism, Alex Rosenberg makes the case that many of “life’s persistent questions” can be answered by science, among them: “Is there a God? No. […] What is the purpose of the universe? There is none. What is the meaning of life? Ditto. Why am I here? Just dumb luck.” It is no coincidence that these answers closely mimic the diagnosis provided by (the atheists among) existentialist thinkers. This line of argument is common in at least the atheistic tradition of existentialism.

But in the face of evil and chaos, it is questionable whether, even with the existence of a supposed deity, our lives are bestowed with any meaning. Theistic existentialists like Kierkegaard, Shestov, and Jaspers would deny such.

The absurd stems from the fact that though life is without meaning and the universe devoid of purpose, man still longs for meaning, significance, and purpose. For existential thinkers like Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Sartre, and Camus, this conflict was central to their philosophy.

If you enjoyed this short essay, you might enjoy the much longer version, on which it is based, where I go into much more detail: click here.

Rosenberg, A. (2011). The Atheist’s Guide to Reality: Enjoying Life without Illusions. New York: W. W. Norton & Company.

Veit, W. (2024). Reclaiming Moral Nihilism. Revista de Filosofía, 49(2), 597–613. https://doi.org/10.5209/resf.91005 [Download]

#4717. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

We moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are currently midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

For all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — also carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4715. A baby turkey with a feather duster ‘mom’ has a new BFF

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 14, 2026 10:03 AM EST

It seems straight out of a Disney movie—wild animals from two different species becoming inseparable friends. And yet that’s what happened at the Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in southeastern Pennsylvania, between a turkey and a mourning dove.

Last spring, the wildlife center received two likely orphaned turkey poults (young turkeys). To calm them down, the team put them with a feather-duster as a stand-in mother turkey. Because turkey poults are easily stressed, they are difficult to rehabilitate, according to a Facebook post by the wildlife center. In fact, one of them didn’t make it.

“Since we never raise baby animals alone, we had to find a companion for the remaining poult,” the wildlife center wrote. “We paired it with a baby mourning dove of similar size, hoping they would comfort each other while eating and exploring as they are both ground eaters.”

The pairing turned out to be a raging success. They formed an inseparable bond that Raven Ridge Wildlife Center had never seen before. Months later, the team gave the dove a soft release, meaning the bird could leave whenever it wanted. But he clearly had no intention of leaving his friend. The dove continued returning to the turkey’s cage, and the two would sit near each other on either side of the separation.

“After a few days, we put the dove back in with the turkey, and it was clear they were happiest together,” the wildlife center explained. But “we knew keeping them caged for the rest of their lives, or keeping them just because they were cute, was neither an option nor fair to these wild animals.”

As such, the team contacted a large sanctuary in Pennsylvania to request a joint release. This way, the duo could choose whether to stick together or follow their own paths. After their soft release, the dove flew into the trees and the turkey started foraging, free to stick together or join other members of their species.

“We don’t know if they’ll stay together, but our team made sure they had a safe place until they were ready to be on their own,” the wildlife center concluded.

#4714. Rejecting Oppression, Embracing Joy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

What makes a literary character—or a living person you’ve just met—seem intensely human? Besides the movements people make and the sensations they describe, their attitudes can show their humanity. In literature, characters who resist social oppression make more compelling protagonists than those who quietly occupy a society's bottom rungs. Most inspiring of all may be characters shocked by abuse because, despite poverty, sexism, and racism, they believe they deserve joyful lives.

In a recent study of over 400 readers, 19 percent reported “experiential crossing” in which the language and characters of a book they were reading entered their daily lives. “It’s as if the character has started to narrate my world,” wrote one participant (Alderson-Day et al. 2017). Getting to know literary characters can broaden readers’ understandings of human life if those characters’ experiences differ from readers' own.

When characters’ experiences match those of readers, their crossover into readers’ worlds can feel life-affirming, especially if their experiences rarely appear in published fiction. At a book signing in Cambridge, a woman thanked author Junot Díaz for creating Beli, a central character in his novel The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao. “I had a life a lot like Beli’s,” the reader told him. Tears kept her from saying more (Díaz 2018).

Born in the Dominican Republic, Belicia (Beli) Cabral is sold as a child after her mother dies and her father is imprisoned for offending the dictator, Rafael Trujillo. During her nine years as a slave, her “father” burns her back with hot oil when she tries to attend school. After a distant relative rescues Beli, she grows into a tall, strikingly beautiful young woman. A relationship with Trujillo’s brother-in-law wrecks her life, however, when his henchmen force her to have an abortion and beat her nearly to death. She escapes to New Jersey, where she marries, but her husband abandons her and their two children. To support her son and daughter, she works several minimum-wage jobs, persisting even after she develops breast cancer. Beli is abusive and violent not just to her children but to neighbors, shoppers, and police officers. Throughout her life, she retains her sense of self-worth, refusing to believe she should be exploited because she is female, Dominican, and Black.

Recent studies affirm that the suppressed emotions caused by social inequality harm people’s physical and mental health (Kiehl 2024). The effects of racism have received more attention than those of social class, whose influence many people still deny (Kiehl 2024). Beli and readers who see their lives in hers experience disrespect caused by sexism as well. Her ability to inspire readers stems not from her suffering, however, but from her sense that she is inferior to no one and deserves a good life.

Junot Díaz’s character-narrator, Yunior, hints that Beli can’t see disaster coming because even after being enslaved and burned, she can’t imagine how badly people will treat her. “Like everybody in this damn story,” he writes, “she underestimated the depth of the shit she was in” (Díaz 2007). Beli’s refusal to accept that she is in danger shows not just her sense of self-worth but her belief (at least in her youth) in other people’s goodness. Yunior illustrates her capacity for joy, which blazes forth in her dancing. A complex character, Beli terrorizes her neighborhood and hurts her children, but her humanity is never in doubt. Her will to survive and her rejection of abuse ensure that whether or not readers see themselves in her, she will enter and inhabit their lives.

Like lay readers, psychologists can learn from imagining Beli because in creating characters, authors build models of minds (Alderson-Day et al. 2017; Bernini 2021). Participants in psychological experiments still come disproportionately from “WEIRD” (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) populations, especially North American and European universities (Henrich et al. 2010). Novels like Díaz’s Oscar Wao guide readers to imagine the mental world of a woman who experiences horrors but retains her self-worth and desire for joy. Until scientific studies can include more of the world’s population, literature can complement information revealed through experiments by making a wider range of human experiences imaginable. Most human of all may be the belief that no matter how other people see you, you deserve to thrive.

Alderson-Day, B., Bernini, M., & Fernyhough, C. (2017). Uncharted features and dynamics of reading: Voices, characters, and crossing of experiences. Consciousness and Cognition 49, 98-109.

Bernini, M. (2021). Becket and the Cognitive Method: Mind, Models, and Exploratory Narratives. New York: Oxford University Press.

Díaz, J. (2007). The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao. New York: Penguin.

Díaz, J. (9 April 2018). The silence. The New Yorker, 24-28.

Henrich, J., Heine, S. J., & Norenzayan, A. (2010). The weirdest people in the world? Behavioral and Brain Sciences 33 (2-3), 61-83.

Kiehl, E. (2024). Social trauma. The Complexity of Trauma: Jungian and Psychoanalytic Approaches to the Treatment of Trauma. Edited by L. Zoppi & M. Schmidt. London: Routledge, pp. 207-26.

#4713. Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on the SSP

After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.

As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.

The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.

“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” Schäfer said in the memo reviewed by Reuters. The Wolfsburg plant, AKA the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.

Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer announced earlier this year that the long-awaited electric car was delayed until closer to 2030.

Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), which is being developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected, again due to costs.

According to Autocar, Volkswagen is now delaying the Audi A4 E-tron as well, another vehicle that was initially planned to be among the first based on the SSP platform.

Production of the electric A4 is being pushed back until at least 2029, a year later than originally planned. While the delay is disappointing for Audi fans (including myself) still waiting for an electric A4, it also puts Audi behind rival luxury brands in the mid-size sedan segment.

BMW has the new i3, and Mercedes-Benz has the C-Class EV, both of which feature major improvements in range, charging, and efficiency over their previous-generation EVs.

Volkswagen said in 2023 that the 800V SSP will serve as a “single future backbone with integrated electric and electronics architecture,” claiming that more than 40 million models were expected to be built on it.

The company also said investment and R&D costs were expected to be reduced by about 30% compared to the current MEB platform, enabling most models “to achieve the same margin compared to their conventionally powered counterparts.”

Volkswagen’s software struggles started in its internal division, Cariad, leading to delays, missed targets, and budget overruns.

To fix it, VW turned to Rivian, forming a joint venture to develop its next-gen software-defined vehicle (SDV) electrical architecture.

In March, VW said several test vehicles, including the ID.EVERY1, Audi, and Scout with the SDV architecture underwent “comprehensive evaluation,” and successfully validated over-the-air (OTA) functionality.

Being cash efficient is good, but delays to the next-gen platform that will keep you competitive with rival brands seem like a problem.

However, the Audi A4 E-tron delay is not entirely about software. The Autocar report claims Audi demanded significant changes to the SSP platform for the A4 E-tron so it more closely matched the current gas version.

Audi reportedly wanted individual footwells for front and rear passengers, which would require repositioning the battery.

The luxury brand also reportedly asked for a 48V electrical system instead of the traditional 12V setup initially planned.

While development of the Golf EV is on hold, VW’s works council said the pause will not delay its launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030. The Audi A4 E-tron is now expected to arrive around 2029.

#4712. How Non-Dairy Creamers Doubled Coffee’s Calories For Many Americans

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

By 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

The researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

The researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she said.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:

“These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” said Kirkpatrick.

She also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick said.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an important factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” said Kirkpatrick.

#4711. 7 apps that really show what the new Apple iPhone Duo can do

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 14, 2026 1:00 PM EST

It took a while, but Apple has finally launched its first foldable: the iPhone Duo is now available in Star White or Night Sky finishes, starting at $1,999 and up, depending on how much storage you want inside.

Apple has built a variety of adaptations into iOS to support the iPhone Duo, so icons and menus will shift if the software detects it’s running on the inner or outer display of the foldable, rather than a standard iPhone. In addition, iOS developers are updating their own apps to better suit the two new screen sizes introduced by the foldable.

We’re also seeing several apps built or optimized specifically for the iPhone Duo, to take advantage of that foldable screen. Whether you’ve got the phone or not, they’re worth checking out as a showcase of what’s possible with the new form factor.

Toastie ($2.99) is a rather whimsical game for the iPad, iPhone, and iPhone Duo. The aim is to make the best grilled sandwich you can, and on Apple’s foldable phone you snap the handset shut and open it again to control the cooking time for your toasties.

You can pick different ingredients and bread types as you go, and the ability to partially open the iPhone Duo to peek at your culinary creation is a nice touch. It’s not the most sophisticated cooking sim, but you might be surprised by how much fun it is to play.

Bring some old-school to your iPhone Duo with Tiny Computers ($3.99): With the foldable half open and propped up, the flat half turns into a virtual keyboard, and the vertical half shows a simulated display from a classic computer of your choice—with 10 to pick from.

The available computers include vintage Windows and Mac machines, plus the Commodore 64; while these aren’t full-scale emulators, you can play around with them and discover some “nostalgic secrets” as you go (including some iconic keyboard sounds).

There are also gaming experiences specifically for the iPhone Duo to enjoy. Marbles Unhinged (freemium, $2.99 to unlock all levels) is a marble-rolling game that uses your phone’s accelerometer and gyroscope to create realistic physical tilting controls.

With the iPhone Duo half open, one half of the main display becomes the marble maze, and the other half becomes a ramp you use to get the marble moving to the right place at the right speed. There are 10 levels available to play for free before you have to pay.

Simply put, Foldissimo (free, $9.99 to unlock all the songs) turns your iPhone Duo into a virtual accordion. You can adjust the airflow affecting the instrument by folding and unfolding the Apple device—faster folds pump in more air and increase the volume.

There is a selection of classic song tutorials included to get you started, and you can compose your own too. You can also switch to other instruments, including panpipes and a theremin, but that’ll cost you extra. A clever idea, neatly implemented.

If you’ve got a hankering for the days when we carried camcorders around as separate gadgets—rather than just using our phones to record video—then Flipcorder ($4.99) is a perfect iPhone Duo app, complete with a retro-looking interface and workflow.

You can only record videos in 20-second bursts, up to 30 minutes a day, reflecting the limitations of camcorders of yesteryear. When you close the foldable, the outer display shows your subjects what’s being filmed, which is a smart touch. (And don’t forget to back your videos up.)

If you remember the Walkman era, then you’ll love Deck-Man ($4.99), which gives the iPhone Duo the feel of a classic cassette player. It interfaces with Apple Music and any music files you’ve got stored locally on your device to give audio playback a retro feel.

Your albums show up as cassette tapes, and there are chunky virtual buttons for starting and stopping the audio—with the familiar fast forward, rewind, and eject buttons here too. The app even includes authentic mechanical sounds, recorded from a real cassette player.

Unfold Your City (free; $4.99 to unlock all the cities) utilizes the iPhone Duo’s foldable form factor to turn the handset into a virtual pop-up book that serves as your guide to the world’s most famous cities. You can even switch between day and night modes.

It’s a fresh twist on the usual travel guide format, and plenty of care and attention has been put into the details here (nice touches include a Tower Bridge that actually opens in London). Be warned, though: the app may have a serious impact on your travel budget.

#4709. The Naked Truth About Taking Your Inner Ape for a Walk

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

Walking is a key milestone for human development, an activity done for recreation, and can be an Olympic sport. Walking is a critical and integral behavior across the animal kingdom. It's also something that can be leveraged with deliberate practice. And it's been going on for millions of years since our proto-human ancestors were learning to stand upright, walk bipedally, and land on their heels.

A key characteristic of human gait is that we land on our heels at the end of swing—something found also in African apes. My research career included diving deep into the neuromechanics of human walking and especially the way sensory feedback and spinal cord motor control vary functionally while we move. I was fascinated by the fact that the most critically controlled part of the step cycle is heel strike—just when your foot lands and weight begins to shift onto the new stance leg.

So my eye was drawn to the recent work, "Heel-strike Mechanics Reveal Evolutionary Trade-offs in Hominin Bipedalism" by Nicholas B. Holowka et al.

These researchers studied bipedal and quadrupedal locomotion of chimpanzees and humans and examined forces and angles of the foot at the beginning of stance. They found that chimpanzees had much larger ranges of foot-strike angles than humans and often did not land heel-first.

Impact forces and loading rates are much higher with heel-striking, but metabolic cost is lower. This work suggests that the primitive leg anatomy of early hominins meant either high impact forces or poor walking economy. A convergent solution for less mechanically stressful, more economical, and larger travel ranges arrived via "evolution of larger heels and lower limb joints."

But can we turn heel-strike walking into striking with our heels? The timing of when you put your foot down at heel strike is the most dangerous part of the entire step cycle. If we make a mistake, or we slip on something, or the ground gives when we put our heel down and our body begins to shift weight onto that leg, we can have a catastrophic failure and a fall. Which is the ultimate failure for the locomotive system.

So it's critical to avoid a catastrophe, and evolution of bipedal locomotion has incorporated neurological connections that assist in controlling this. But the opposite side of that is that it's also an opportunity. And that's where self-protection and martial arts training factor in.

That critical part of the step cycle is an excellent time to take that heel and stomp it onto an attacker's instep or the top of their foot. You can jam all your weight that's already moving forward to normally be accepted by your stance leg. But now it's to destabilize your opponent.

This is something I teach when guiding martial arts practice: harnessing the natural movement of the body as the base layer for tactical reaction. Martial arts like Bagua Zhang center core practice on circle walking, where locomotion is central to the performance of discrete actions. We can connect our evolutionary advantage in walking to become a powerful application of self-protective action. This allows us to fully express the functional connectivity within the nervous system, mostly subliminal and automatic, in deliberate mindful action.

Holowka NB, O'Neill MC, Bhandal V, Lam O, Apolito ZM, Massimi CA, Palmisano KG, Worthington S, Demes B, Thompson NE. Heel-strike mechanics reveal evolutionary trade-offs in hominin bipedalism. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2026 Sep 15;123(37):e2533918123. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2533918123. Epub 2026 Sep 8. PMID: 42709797.

Zehr EP, Barss TS, Dragert K, Frigon A, Vasudevan EV, Haridas C, Hundza S, Kaupp C, Klarner T, Klimstra M, Komiyama T, Loadman PM, Mezzarane RA, Nakajima T, Pearcey GE, Sun Y. Neuromechanical interactions between the limbs during human locomotion: an evolutionary perspective with translation to rehabilitation. Exp Brain Res. 2016 Nov;234(11):3059-3081. doi: 10.1007/s00221-016-4715-4. Epub 2016 Jul 15. PMID: 27421291; PMCID: PMC5071371.

#4708. Can squirrels really survive any fall?

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 15, 2026 7:54 AM EST

On any ordinary day, you might witness the breathtaking display of squirrels high in the trees, doing what seems like effortless, daredevilish parkour. They might launch themselves off one branch, bounce off another, and somehow reorient themselves in midair like it’s nothing.

A large, heavy human being attempting these same maneuvers would likely fall—and would be looking at a trip to the E.R., at best.

Yet squirrels, it seems, tend to walk away from these situations unscathed. You’ve probably even heard that squirrels can survive a fall from any height. But according to Dr. Nathaniel Hunt of the University of Nebraska at Omaha, this comes with an important caveat: Even these brazen little gymnasts don’t stick the landing every single time.

“I would put an asterisk on the claim that squirrels can survive a fall from literally any height,” Hunt tells Popular Science. “Their size makes large falls surprisingly survivable, but they are not invulnerable.”

So, can squirrels survive, if not all, most falls? And if so, how?

It’s much more than luck that keeps squirrels landing safely; they are no more immune than we are to the laws of gravity. It’s what happens in the air—both in terms of their anatomical engineering and their instincts—that allows them to survive most falls and get right back to their nut-hiding hijinks.

According to Hunt, a falling squirrel faces three challenges: the speed of the fall, its orientation midair, and the impact when it lands. A squirrel’s small body helps; at about a pound, a squirrel weighs about as much as a loaf of bread.

“Being small gives it a lot of aerodynamic area relative to its weight, so air resistance limits its speed,” Hunt says. “It also has much less kinetic energy than a larger animal.”

So, squirrels’ light and small bodies help them hit the ground with less force, but that’s not all that’s going on. Hunt says squirrels instinctively know how to move through the air and land on the ground, which helps to optimize their already “favorable physics.” The tail is a key player in these midair maneuvers.

“The tail is more interesting than a fluffy parachute,” Hunt notes. “At low airspeeds, aerodynamic forces are small, but the squirrel can still use inertial tail movements to exchange angular momentum with the body and control orientation.” In other words, squirrels use their tail to control how and where they fall.

Research backs Hunt’s claim. A 2021 study found that squirrels experiencing unexpected falls were able to rapidly rotate their tails, a motion that caused the rest of their bodies to rotate in the opposite direction. Hunt compared the role of the tail to that of a “reaction wheel” on a spacecraft.

“Accelerating the tail in one direction helps rotate or stabilize the body in the other direction,” Hunt says.

As a squirrel’s fall picks up speed, the tail may function more like the feathers on an arrow, Hunt suggests. If the squirrel starts to veer off course, the airflow pushes against the tail just enough to redirect its body into a stable position. Even then, the tail isn’t acting like a true parachute; instead of slowing the squirrel’s descent, the tail is nudging its body in the right direction.

Size, anatomy, and aerial reorientation are all important to a squirrel’s seemingly magical ability to survive most falls. However, there’s a third skill that plays an equally important part, one Hunt thinks may be “the most underappreciated part of the story.” Squirrels know how to come in for a landing.

“A recent study I co-authored found that fox squirrels managed more than 80 percent of their landing energy through their forelimbs,” Hunt says of a study looking at squirrels leaping between branches. “They also adjusted their forces depending on whether they undershot or overshot the branch.”

In other words, a landing isn’t just something that happens to a squirrel. On some level, they’re doing damage control.

“They are not simply hitting the branch,” Hunt says. “They are actively controlling the collision.”

So, how slowly does a squirrel have to fall to be able to walk away?

The answer lies in our furry friend’s terminal velocity, the top speed something reaches while falling once air resistance balances gravity’s pull and stops it from accelerating further. Hunt says a squirrel’s terminal velocity can be reasonably estimated at about 20 to 40 mph, depending on its posture, limb position, and tail. For reference, Hunt estimates the terminal velocity of a cat—famous nine lives aside—at about 60 mph, while a belly-down human skydiver is likely to fall at about 120 mph.

“All of these are approximate, because posture matters enormously,” he says.

Posture explains some of the variation, but size is ultimately the main driver. A giant squirrel, therefore, would likely fare much worse in a fall, even with perfect tail control and posture.

“You could not simply build a squirrel 10 times larger and expect it to tolerate the same fall,” Hunt says.

Likewise, a squirrel’s comparatively slow terminal velocity doesn’t mean it’s out of the proverbial woods. It might seem that once a squirrel hits its maximum speed, height wouldn’t matter much, making a fall from 10 feet and a fall from 100 feet equally survivable. Hunt cautions against assumptions like this.

“Reaching terminal velocity does not make a squirrel immune to injury,” he says. “The landing surface, body orientation, and any collisions along the way still matter.”

This complex interplay of physics, instinct, learning, and split-second decision-making is part of what makes squirrels a fascinating study subject for Hunt.

“What fascinates me is that you cannot neatly separate ‘the brain’ from ‘the mechanics,'” Hunt says. “Squirrel agility emerges from sensing, learning, body shape, and physical dynamics working together.”
